clue.text: A rascal, one of the small fry

parts.note: a scamp is a young rascal or rogue
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A young rogue is dismissed as just one more of life's small fry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small fry' looks like insignificant people, but it means little sea creatures; scampi are small lobster-like shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are small shellfish, the Norway lobster, so literally a kind of small marine fry.

clue.text: Preside at table-the Doones' perhaps?

parts.note: the head of a household presides at table by slicing the roast

explanation.surface: Who sits at the head of the table in the outlaw Doone family?
explanation.walkthrough: In Blackmore's novel Lorna Doone the brutal Carver Doone is a leading member of the outlaw clan; the host who slices the Sunday joint does the same job.
explanation.definitionFit: The person presiding at a family meal traditionally slices the roast meat for everyone.

clue.text: The rope for Jack in the same difficulty

indicators.note: a difficulty is a mess or tangle, so the letters before it are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor finds himself in exactly the same trouble with his rigging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' is a sailor (Jack tar). 'difficulty' works on IN plus THE SAME, rearranging all nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mainsheet is the line controlling a yacht's mainsail, a rope every sailor handles.

clue.text: One offer upsets me in the same place

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
a bid is an offer at an auction

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsets turns the word me upside down, so it reads from the bottom

explanation.surface: Someone's single offer annoys me in the same spot as before.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibidem is the Latin footnote term, abbreviated ibid., used for a reference to a source just cited.

clue.text: Sinister character who becomes a whistler in the dark?

definitions.text: Sinister character who becomes a whistler in the dark?

parts.words: Sinister character who becomes a whistler in the dark?
parts.note: a wolf is a man who whistles at women, and a monster of legend turns into a wolf at night

explanation.surface: A shady figure who whistles nervously when the lights go out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistling in the dark' suggests nervous bravado, but a 'wolf' is a man who wolf-whistles; the legendary man-beast becomes a wolf after dark.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore a lycanthrope is a man who changes into a wolf at nightfall, a sinister figure of horror.

clue.text: Revolutionary Mohammedan

parts.note: read not as a political rebel but as a Muslim who literally revolves, spinning in religious dance

explanation.surface: A Muslim rebel seeks to overthrow the state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests a political rebel; here it means one who turns round and round, as Sufi dancers of the Mevlevi order do in worship.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a Sufi order spin continuously in ecstatic dance as an act of devotion.

clue.text: The herrings go round and round

definitions.text: The herrings go round and round

parts.words: The herrings go round and round
parts.note: the fish fillets are rolled up round a filling, so the herrings literally go round and round

explanation.surface: A shoal of herrings swims in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is fish circling in the sea; the dish is pickled herring fillets rolled around onion or gherkin.
explanation.definitionFit: These are pickled herring fillets curled into cylinders around a savoury filling.

clue.text: It's all so stagey !

parts.note: recalls Shakespeare's line from As You Like It that everything is a stage; the thing that is all a stage is the whole earth

explanation.surface: A complaint that everything is terribly theatrical.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques in As You Like It says 'All the ___'s a stage'; the clue turns that into 'it is all a stage'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's famous speech the whole of earthly existence is compared to a theatre stage.

clue.text: Under the City thoroughfare one finds rock

indicators.note: in a down clue the word one is placed beneath the street, so it comes after it

parts.note: Lime Street, abbreviated Lime St, runs through the City of London
taken as written

explanation.surface: Beneath a street in London's financial district, solid rock is found.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, where Lime Street (home of Lloyd's) runs.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a sedimentary rock formed mostly of calcium carbonate, such as chalk.

clue.text: It isn't natural!

parts.note: a plain description of anything made by humans rather than by nature

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something is unnatural.
explanation.definitionFit: Something man-made or synthetic is by definition not produced by nature.

clue.text: The end of Parliament?

parts.note: the backside is an end, and the remnant of the Long Parliament after Pride's Purge of 1648 had the same name

explanation.surface: Is this the dissolution of Parliament?
explanation.walkthrough: 'End' suggests closure, but it means the hind end; the Rump Parliament was what was left of the Long Parliament after it was purged in 1648.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear end or buttocks of an animal shares its name with the remnant English Parliament of 1648-53.

clue.text: "It's lovely when you're in !" On the contrary, says the pick-up on the beach!

definitions.text: "It's lovely when you're in !" On the contrary, says the pick-up on the beach!

parts.words: "It's lovely when you're in !" On the contrary, says the pick-up on the beach!
parts.note: the bather's cry that the water is lovely is contradicted: the item found on the sand, split as a phrase, says the sea is hell

explanation.surface: A swimmer insists the water is lovely, but a beachcomber disagrees.
explanation.walkthrough: Swimmers call 'it's lovely once you're in'; split the beach find as SEA'S HELL and it says the opposite. 'Pick-up' is a thing picked up on the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: A shell from a sea creature is the typical object picked up along the shore.

clue.text: Fashionable doctor meets a pretty girl

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor
a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: A trendy doctor meets an attractive young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Modish means in the current style, stylish and up to date.

clue.text: A piece is easy, but winner takes all

definitions.text: A piece is easy, but winner takes all

parts.words: A piece is easy, but winner takes all
parts.note: two idioms: a piece of this is something easy, and the winner takes this, meaning carries off the prize

explanation.surface: A statement about a contest where a portion is easy but the champion claims everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A piece of ___' means something easy; 'takes the ___' means wins the prize (from cakewalk contests).
explanation.definitionFit: The idioms 'piece of' and 'takes the' both use this baked dessert to mean easy and winning.

clue.text: Evince disgust at bomber's 12½% score, we hear?

indicators.note: signals that the phrase from the wordplay is to be spoken and only its sound kept

parts.note: 12½% is one in eight, so the bomber's score is one bomb in eight: a bomb in eight

explanation.surface: Show contempt for a bomber who hits only one target in eight.
explanation.walkthrough: 12½% is one eighth; a bomber scoring that lands 'a bomb in eight', which said quickly gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe or detest something is to show strong disgust at it.

clue.text: Twenty francs a game

definitions.meaning: the gold ... was a French coin worth twenty francs
a card game related to nap in which players bid tricks

explanation.definitionFit: Named after the emperor, the word covers both a French gold coin worth twenty francs and a trick-taking card game.

clue.text: " To scorn delights, and live — days" (Milton)

definitions.text: " To scorn delights, and live — days" (Milton)

parts.words: " To scorn delights, and live — days" (Milton)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Milton's Lycidas: the missing word describes days of hard toil

explanation.surface: A line of Milton on renouncing pleasure for a life of toil.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Milton's elegy Lycidas: 'To scorn delights, and live ___ days', about the scholar's dedication.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective means toilsome, full of hard work, the days of a dedicated scholar.

clue.text: A chap takes it up, all upset over a senorita

indicators.note: the man takes on what follows, so the next piece is attached directly after him

parts.note: a chap is a man

indicators.note: in a down clue taking something up turns the word it to read from the bottom

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the word all upside down

explanation.surface: A man lifts something and spills everything over a Spanish girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns IT to TI and 'upset' turns ALL to LLA, both reading upwards in the down clue. The definition says where the garment goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantilla is a lace scarf worn draped over the head and shoulders by Spanish women.

clue.text: An example of seaside rudery perhaps?

definitions.text: An example of seaside rudery perhaps?

parts.words: An example of seaside rudery perhaps?
parts.note: British resorts sell saucy cartoon cards to mail home, famous for their cheeky double meanings

explanation.surface: Bad behaviour at the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: British seaside resorts are famous for 'saucy' picture cards with innuendo, such as Donald McGill's, sent home by holidaymakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic cards with risqué cartoons are a traditional British holiday item mailed from the coast.

clue.text: "And murmuring of innumerable" (Tennyson)

parts.note: the line from Tennyson's The Princess ends with the humming insects heard among elms

explanation.surface: A quotation from Tennyson on endless murmuring.
explanation.walkthrough: From Tennyson's The Princess: 'The moan of doves in immemorial elms, / And murmuring of innumerable ___'.
explanation.definitionFit: The humming insects of Tennyson's line are honey-making insects buzzing in the trees.

clue.text: Rough in Paris for the Indian

definitions.meaning: a rough is a thug, and in Paris a street ruffian was so called
a Native American people of the south-west United States

explanation.definitionFit: The Native American people lent their name to Parisian street gangsters of the early 1900s.

clue.text: Tasty morsel on the bird-table?

parts.note: a delicacy, read as a scrap left for a small garden songbird

explanation.surface: A treat put out for garden birds.
explanation.walkthrough: A titbit is a tasty morsel; read as TIT BIT it is a bit for a tit, a small garden bird visiting a feeding table.
explanation.definitionFit: A titbit is a small choice piece of food, a delicacy.

clue.text: He makes something to break

parts.note: the tradesman bakes loaves, which are broken and shared at meals

explanation.surface: A man who creates things only so they can be broken.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's last word is a rearrangement of the answer's own letters, a hint; bread is what is broken.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who bakes bread produces loaves that are broken and shared.

clue.text: Bank proprietor is right with one kind of marble

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
Parian marble is the fine white marble from the Greek island of Paros

explanation.surface: A banker is right to be investing in a particular type of marble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank proprietor' looks financial, but it is a river bank: a riparian owner holds land on a riverbank.
explanation.definitionFit: In law a riparian is the owner of land alongside a river, a riverbank holder.

clue.text: Sailor on horseback loses direction to 14

indicators.note: in a down clue the sailor sits on top of what follows, so comes first

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: loses means the letters for a compass direction are taken away

parts.note: on horseback is on a horse, so the word gives horse
SE, south-east, is a compass direction

explanation.surface: A sailor riding a horse gets lost and is disgusted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' takes SE (south-east) from HORSE, leaving HOR. 14 is ABOMINATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To abominate and to abhor are synonyms, both meaning to detest or loathe.

clue.text: Not heart of oak, this ship!

definitions.meaning: the outer covering of a tree trunk, the opposite of its heartwood
a three-masted sailing vessel, also spelled barque

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a tree's outer skin, as against its heartwood, and a sailing vessel.

clue.text: Primitive wear for clergy beset by wild lions

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded, so the clergy word goes inside the jumbled letters
wild means the letters of lions run riot into a new order

parts.note: the cloth is a collective term for the clergy

explanation.surface: Ministers surrounded by wild lions in an arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primitive wear' sounds like tools, but it is clothing. 'wild' rearranges the big cats into LOINS, and 'beset by' puts the clergy inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: Simple cloths wrapped about the hips are the basic garment of early or tribal peoples.

clue.text: Censure concerning a quiet fish

parts.note: re means concerning or about
p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
a roach is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A rebuke about a silent fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To reproach someone is to rebuke or express disapproval of them.

clue.text: Make certain of three points by the river

indicators.note: by means next to, so the river follows the points

parts.note: E, N and S are compass points: east, north and south
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Secure three positions beside the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To guarantee or secure an outcome is to make sure it happens.
